beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer — the ask lands answered
beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on tutor mode: how the physics engine helps a student without handing over the answer. Every chatbot can give you the answer. The harder thing is giving you the next step, and only the next step, and making sure every step is right.

props.command: How does the physics engine's tutor mode give hints without giving away the answer?
output: Seven hints, each revealing a little more
Built from the plan, not a second AI call
The answer comes last, and it's verified

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes, you'll see three things. First, the badge every answer wears when the engine is switched on. Second, the hint ladder, rung by rung, on a real problem. And third, why the hints got better when the math went symbolic. No physics or coding background needed.

First, the switch. With Physics Engine mode on, every answer arrives with a badge. Verified: a symbolic solver computed this. Needs review: more than one principle fits, so here's each result. Unverified: nothing in the library covers this, so this is A.I. reasoning. In the team's words, that visible status is the product.

And there's a floor. On the unverified path, the student is no worse off than with the switch off, because that path is the switch off, labeled. So there's no question where turning it on makes the answer worse. And an unverified answer can never leave the engine wearing a verified label.

Now tutor mode. Take the pulley: masses of four and six kilograms. Hint one: here's what you're given, and what you're solving for. Hint two: this is a dynamics problem, and the principle is the Atwood machine. Hint three: check the conditions first. A frictionless, massless pulley, and a string that doesn't stretch. Hint four: the relationships you need, one equation for each mass.

Hint five: the common mistake to avoid. Inconsistent signs across the two masses' equations. Hint six: the formula rearranged for what you want. Acceleration equals g, times m two minus m one, over m one plus m two. And only then, hint seven: the worked result. One point nine six meters per second squared, and a tension of forty-seven point zero four newtons.

beats.new_visual_element: from the plan, withheld on purpose
beats.narration_text: Every hint is built from the plan the engine already made: the card, its conditions, its equations, its warning. There's no second model call, so a hint can't invent a step. In tutor mode the engine also holds back the answer, the equations, and even the card's name, because the name gives away hint two. Each rung reveals strictly less than the next.

Something the team didn't expect. When the math went symbolic, the hints got better. Hint four used to read, T minus thirty-nine point two equals four a. The arithmetic had already leaked. Now it reads, T minus g m one equals a m one. It teaches the relationship. And caching made it faster: about six milliseconds a problem, down from eleven. What's not proven: no student has used it yet.
So here's the takeaway. A good tutor gives you the next step, not the last one. When you study with an A.I. model, ask for one hint at a time, and try each step yourself before asking for the next.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude with a problem you're stuck on. It asks Claude to tutor you the way the engine does.

props.command: Tutor me on this problem: [paste it]. Do not give the answer. Give one hint at a time, in this order: what is given and asked; the principle; the conditions it needs; the equations; the common mistake; the rearranged formula; the result. Wait for me after each hint.

beats.new_visual_element: title restate, terracotta period, name beneath
beats.narration_text: The next step, not the last one. This has been Param Madan. Thanks for watching.
